newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 10.

text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- VW AND GM END BITTER THREE-YEAR ROW OVER 'SPYING'

Automotive giants Volkswagen and General Motors have agreed a deal to end a bitter three-year dispute over alleged industrial espionage. An out-of-court settlement has been agreed to, which involves VW paying $100 million to GM and undertaking to buy $1.0 billion in parts from the U.S. company over the next seven years.
-- LITTLEWOODS DROPS 135 MILLION STG EXPANSION PLAN

Littlewoods has made a major u-turn in its business strategy by scrapping plans for a 135 million sterling expansion of department stores. Last year, the firm -- Britain's largest privately-held company -- announced plans to open up to nine stores a year for the next five years. But the plans, which would have created about 3,000 jobs, has been scrapped in favour of a concentration on home shopping following a review from a firm of management consultants.
-- STRONG POUND CUTS PROFITS FORECASTS FOR BIG EXPORTERS

The strength of sterling is continuing to cause concern for British industry, with brokers for British Steel and ICI -- two of the country's biggest exporters -- reducing their forecasts for profits. Investment house Merrill Lynch cut its forecast for British Steel to 280 million sterling pre-tax from 650 million stg purely on concerns about currencies. Brokers HSBC James Capel cut ICI's forecast profits for 1997 by 100 million sterling to 750 million stg pre tax.
-- TOO LATE TO START DEFUSING COMPUTER DATE BOMB

The executive director of Taskforce 2000, the group of experts set up by the government to tackle the problem of older computers switching dates from 1999 to 2000, says companies that have not yet overhauled their systems to cope with the problem have left it too late. Robin Guenier said companies should have a revised system operating by October 1998. A number of major companies, including BT and Pearson, are now insisting that their suppliers are able to demonstrate that they have modified their own systems.
-- HOME STARTS RISE TO HIGHEST LEVEL FOR SEVEN YEARS

Environment Minister James Clappison says the number of new homes started by private sector builders last autumn was the highest since 1989. Clappison said 42,000 new homes were begun in the three months to the end of November, a 39 percent increase over the same period in 1995. Retailers have reported an increase in demand for household goods following the recent improvement in property sales and house prices.
-- BNFL WINS $1.1 BILLION U.S. CONTRACT

British Nuclear Fuels Ltd (BNFL) has led the successful consortium in the bidding for an estimated $1.1 billion contract to dispose of waste from the production of U.S. atomic weapons. BNFL, the state-owned nuclear fuel reprocessor and waste management company, said its U.S. subsidiary BNFL Inc is likely to gain most of the revenue from the contract, which has been awarded by the U.S. Department of Energy.
-- SEARS CHIEF'S FATE UNSURE AFTER PROFITS WARNING

Sears, the retail group, has issued a warning that this year's profits are likely to be significantly lower than last year's 100 million stg. The warning has put a question mark over the future of the group's chief executive, Liam Strong, with a number of leading shareholders seeking a meeting with Sears chairman Sir Bob Reid following publication of the disappointing trading statement.
-- REG VARDY THRIVES IN SLACK MARKET

Automotive retailer Reg Vardy has reported a 28 percent rise in interim pre-tax profits, excluding exceptionals, to 7.86 million stg. The group, Britian's largest car dealer, has grown rapidly since it was set up 14 years ago, doubling in size every three years, and is planning to increase its dealerships to 60 from 43 following a rights issue last year. Sales for the period rose 21 percent, despite sluggish growth in the British car market.
-- S&F LAUNCHES FIRST FOOTBALL FUND

The current infatuation of the City with the sport of football has been underlined with the launch of the country's first specialist football investment trust. Merchant bank Singer & Friedlander have launched the Football Fund as an open-ended investment company with the intention of investing in British and continental European clubs and companies with a high level of involvement in football-related activities.
